title: The spy game is changing. And US soldiers are ‘prime targets.’
text:
The spy game is changing. And US soldiers are ‘prime targets.’
The arrest of a senior soldier is adding to concerns about members of the U.S. military being recruited by spies.
The arrest in England of a senior U.S. Army officer, suspected of spying for Russia, underlines the increasingly urgent warnings coming from top U.S. commanders: Foreign intelligence agencies are working hard to recruit American soldiers.
Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner was working at a British army base in Gloucestershire, which hosts NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, when he was taken into custody in early November.
If an offer “seems flattering, urgent, exclusive, or too good to be true, it probably is,” Lt. Gen. Anthony Hale, then the Army’s top spy, told troops in a service-wide memo late last year. He also reminded them of the “swift and real consequences for betraying your oath.”
The FBI says espionage arrests have grown by more than half since early last year, with some of the cases involving U.S. military personnel. With the ease of modern communication, U.S. commanders are issuing urgent warnings about the need for vigilance.
Spying is an ancient pursuit, particularly among great powers. But new technology offers ever trickier methods – from fake job ads on social media to eavesdropping air fryers – for other countries to gather personal information that helps pinpoint potential recruits, military analysts say.
“Espionage is old; the tradecraft is new,” says J.C. Lintzenich, a retired senior military intelligence officer. “Before you had to meet somebody in a dark alley.” While the fundamentals are still there, including the reasons people do it, the speed at which it can happen is much quicker, he adds. “And harder to detect.”
The FBI is now cracking down. Espionage arrests have grown by more than half since early 2025, FBI Director Kash Patel said after the arrest of Colonel Tyner.
Though he has at times been a “harsh critic” of Pentagon policy, Mr. Lintzenich says it “has been responsible in recognizing the pace at which the threats are targeting military personnel.”
”Service members are a prime target”
The range of indictments in recent months highlights the breadth of the U.S. military’s counterintelligence efforts.
A National Guardsman was arrested last October for saying he’d photograph an Army base in Kansas for someone he believed to be a Russian agent. He is also alleged to have procured a military helicopter radio that he planned to help smuggle to Russia.
That followed closely on the heels of the conviction of a former U.S. Army intelligence analyst for selling his unit’s operational orders and technical manuals for missile defense systems to China for a grand total of $42,000. He was recruited through the web by a Chinese agent shortly after receiving top secret security clearance.
Beijing has been “relentless in its efforts to steal our national defense information,” Mr. Patel said at the time, “and service members are a prime target.”
Along with tech-savvy recruiting methods, the Pentagon must also contend with employees unhappy about the policies of the Trump administration.
A computer specialist with the Defense Intelligence Agency reached out to a U.S. European ally offering information in exchange for citizenship because he said he didn’t “expect things here [in the U.S.] to improve in the long term.” He added that he was “not opposed to other compensation.”
In all, counterintelligence arrests against Russian agents are up 25% while prosecutions of Iranian operatives are up 55%, and Chinese spies by 88%, according to FBI figures.
The U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command has, in response, pushed out social media campaigns reminding troops of some basics.
One included a cartoon of a woman next to a bespectacled soldier in a bar. “Are you a spy?” he asked her. “Because you’re way too cute to be talking to me.”
An Army publication last year warned that “even seemingly innocuous smart devices” such as phones and Chinese-made air fryers have microphones and trackers to mine data that could potentially be used against soldiers.
Service members now get mandatory counterintelligence briefings to help them recognize if they’re being recruited by foreign governments through ostensibly legitimate means such as networking sites.
Since late 2023, troops have also been barred from taking certain jobs with some foreign governments and companies after leaving active service. The idea is to keep them from transferring their military skills to U.S. competitors in sectors such as arms manufacturing.
Money, ideology, coercion, and ego
Colonel Tyner was a human resources officer with NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Force, which means he likely wasn’t “sitting there with all the super-classified information,” says Mr. Lintzenich, now a visiting senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States.
Still, he had access to personnel and medical files, which could have made him an appealing recruit for the Russians.
Though the technology has changed, the reasons that spies do what they do have not, analysts point out. Counterintelligence specialists have an acronym for it, MICE: money, ideology, coercion, and ego.
While Colonel Tyner’s alleged motives are yet to be unveiled, what is clear is that spies aren’t generally the James Bond type, Mr. Lintzenich says. “It’s not the flashy operator. It’s the little old lady in tennis shoes. It’s the HR person.”
